Chapter 4: Social Expectations and the Weight of Masculinity
Once you step outside your front door, the world has its own ideas about what it means to be a man—especially during pregnancy. These expectations are everywhere: in everyday conversations, in movies, in the advice your friends and family love to give. Guys are supposed to be strong, reliable, and steady—someone who never gets rattled, even when everything’s changing. But let’s be honest, those ideals? They can feel like a comfort... or a heavy weight to carry.
Take the story of a guy working in a male-dominated office. The minute he shares the news about his partner’s pregnancy, his coworkers start in with the teasing. They joke about sleepless nights ahead and the so-called end of his freedom. But here’s what’s missing—they never actually ask how he feels about becoming a dad. The message is loud and clear: fatherhood is something you just survive, not something to celebrate. And if he shows a hint of nerves or excitement? He gets skepticism or, worse, a little mockery.
This kind of social pressure makes it tough for men to talk honestly about what they’re going through. Nobody wants to look weak or too emotional, so worries stay bottled up. Even in the most supportive circles, there’s often this quiet expectation: put your needs aside for your partner and the baby. Your feelings? They can wait.
And a lot of this gets learned young. If you grew up watching your dad work long hours and rarely show emotion, you might think that’s the only way to be a parent. Balancing work and home starts to feel impossible, and the guilt hits hard when you miss out on milestones. The pressure to provide can totally overshadow the desire to really connect—leaving you feeling kind of alone, even when you’re doing everything “right.”
But here’s some good news: things are changing. More and more men are stepping up, taking an active role in pregnancy and parenting, and pushing back on the idea that it’s just “women’s work.” Some are hitting up childbirth classes, reading parenting books, or taking time off work so they can actually be there for their partner. Others are joining support groups or seeing a counselor—realizing that their own well-being matters just as much as anyone else’s.
There’s this one dad-to-be who’d kept his feelings locked up for years. He finally decided to open up to a close friend about his fears. Turns out, his friend had felt the same way during his own partner’s pregnancy. The conversation was awkward at first, sure, but then something clicked. Both guys realized they weren’t alone—and that asking for help was actually okay.
These little moments of honesty? They can spark real change. When men share their stories, they give others permission to do the same. It chips away at those old stereotypes, and slowly, society starts to see fatherhood less as a burden and more as a chance to grow and connect.
Still, shaking off the weight of social expectations isn’t easy. Even with the most supportive partner or community, old habits die hard. People still expect men to be the rock, the steady hand in the storm. But it takes real courage to push back, to say, “Hey, this is a lot,” and to reach out for support when you need it.
